This is morna. 18th to 19th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The oral tradition places the origins of the morna on Boa Vista Island in the 18th century, potentially evolving from a cross between local working choros and the introduced lundum.
By the 19th century, it was a fully formed genre, with compositions like 'Brada Maria' documented around 1870.
The 2nd period, led by Eugénio Tavares in the early 20th century on Brava Island, introduced slower tempos and romantic lyricism focused on love and separation.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed at key life events such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions.
Central themes include universal subjects like love, as well as distinctively Cape Verdean realities: departure abroad, return, saudade, love for the homeland, and the sea.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: As a dance the morna is a ballroom dance, danced in pairs.
The performers dance with an arm embracing the partner, while with the other arm they hold hands.
The dancing is made through two body swings to one side in a music's bar, while in the next bar the swinging is to the other side.
Watch for The Two-Bar Body Swing.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (aN8KsbFz3jE)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Ballroom dance, danced in pairs

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Characterized by a lento tempo and a 2-beat bar (sometimes 4), traditional morna relies on a harmonic structure based on a cycle of fifths and is almost always monotonic.
The melody features frequent syncopation, extending notes from the end of a bar to the strong beat of the next.
Listen for the guitar (violão), cavaquinho, violin (rabeca), piano.
The pulse is 2-beat bar (sometimes 4) at about 60 beats a minute.

A slow, plaintive acoustic sound led by guitar fingerpicking (*mãozada*) intertwining a steady bass with arpeggiated chords, accompanied by expressive, sorrowful vocals exploring themes of longing and departure.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Cesária Évora, Eugénio Tavares, B. Leza (Francisco Xavier da Cruz), Bana, Celina Pereira, Teté Alhinho, Jorge Monteiro, Manuel de Novas, Ildo Lobo.
Boa Vista morna is the oldest variant, characterized by a quicker tempo (andante ~96 bpm), rubato style, simpler structure, and satirical or social themes.
Considered by some authors to be a cross between local choros and the lundum.

Rhythm pattern: Syncopated, where a note at the end of a bar is extended to the strong beat of the next; accented on the first and last half-beat. Instruments: guitar (violão), cavaquinho, violin (rabeca), piano, clarinet, accordion, ten/twelve-string guitar (viola), percussion. Vocal style: Emotional, lyrical, sung in Cape Verdean Creole. Form: Strophic alternating with a refrain, featuring a solo instrumental intro and a middle instrumental improvisation. Mood: melancholic, nostalgic, romantic, plaintive, saudade. It should sound like this: A slow, plaintive acoustic sound led by guitar fingerpicking (*mãozada*) intertwining a steady bass with arpeggiated chords, accompanied by expressive, sorrowful vocals exploring themes of longing and departure. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.
